title: Robot Explorers and the Road to Mars
summary: Robots went where people could not: past scorching Venus, out beyond the giant planets and even out of the solar system. On Mars, six-wheeled rovers drove for years, and a tiny helicopter made the first flight on another planet.

sections.heading: Sending Robots Instead of People
paragraphs: While astronauts were learning to orbit the Earth and walk on the Moon, a quieter kind of explorer was setting off on much longer journeys. These explorers had no lungs, no stomachs and no families waiting at home. They were robots: boxes of electronics, cameras and radios, folded up on top of rockets and flung toward other planets. Scientists call them space probes, and over the past sixty years they have visited every planet in our solar system.

Why send robots? The answer is mostly about distance and danger. The Moon is about three days away by spacecraft. Mars, at its closest, is more than a hundred times farther than the Moon, and a trip there takes many months. Venus is covered in clouds of acid. Jupiter is wrapped in radiation strong enough to fry a human in a short time. A robot does not need food, water, air or a way home. It can be built small and light, which means a smaller, cheaper rocket can launch it. And if something goes wrong, nobody dies.

Most of the early planetary probes were built by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, usually called JPL, in Pasadena, California, and by Soviet design bureaus such as the Lavochkin company near Moscow. Both sides were racing, just as they were racing to put people in orbit. Both suffered painful failures. In the early 1960s, more probes to Mars and Venus broke down, missed their targets or never left Earth orbit than succeeded. Building a machine that could survive a long trip through cold, empty space, then do its job perfectly at the right moment, turned out to be fiendishly hard.

sections.heading: Venus: Hotter Than an Oven
paragraphs: NASA launched Mariner 1 toward Venus in July 1962, but it veered off course just after liftoff because of a guidance problem, and the range safety officer had to destroy it. Its twin, Mariner 2, launched on 27 August 1962. It was a small craft, about 200 kilograms, with solar panels spread like wings. After a journey of almost four months it swept past Venus on 14 December 1962, passing roughly 35,000 kilometres from the planet. It became the first successful mission to another planet.

Mariner 2 had no camera. Instead it carried instruments that measured invisible microwave and infrared light coming from Venus. Its readings showed that Venus was not a tropical paradise at all. The surface was blazing hot, hundreds of degrees Celsius, far hotter than a kitchen oven. On the way, Mariner 2 also made the first direct measurements of the solar wind, the steady stream of charged particles that flows outward from the Sun. Scientists had predicted it, and now they had proof.

The Soviet Union wanted to go further and land. Its Venera ('Venus' in Russian) probes were built tough, like diving bells, because the air of Venus turned out to be far thicker and hotter than anyone had guessed. After several earlier probes were crushed or failed, Venera 7 reached the surface on 15 December 1970. Its signal was very weak, perhaps because it tipped over or bounced as it landed, and at first controllers thought it had failed. But when scientists studied the recordings carefully, they found it had kept sending faint data from the ground for about twenty minutes. Venera 7 had become the first spacecraft to land on another planet and send information back. It reported a temperature of around 475 degrees Celsius.

Later Venera landers went further. In October 1975, Venera 9 sent back the first pictures ever taken on the surface of another planet: a grey, rocky landscape under a dim orange sky. In 1982, Venera 13 took colour pictures and survived for about two hours before the heat and crushing pressure destroyed it. On the surface of Venus, the air presses down about 90 times harder than air does on Earth, like being nearly a kilometre deep in the ocean. The clouds are made of sulfuric acid, and a thick blanket of carbon dioxide traps heat in a runaway greenhouse effect. Venus taught scientists a sobering lesson about how hot a planet can become.

sections.heading: Mariner 4's Grainy Pictures of Mars
paragraphs: If Venus was hidden behind clouds, Mars seemed to be teasing. Through telescopes it showed red deserts, dark patches that changed with the seasons and white polar caps that grew and shrank. In the late 1800s, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Schiaparelli described 'canali' on Mars, an Italian word meaning channels, and the American astronomer Percival Lowell became convinced they were canals built by intelligent Martians. Science-fiction writers filled Mars with civilisations. Most astronomers were doubtful, but nobody could be sure until a spacecraft went close.

That spacecraft was Mariner 4. It launched from Cape Kennedy (now Cape Canaveral) in Florida on 28 November 1964, and its sister, Mariner 3, had failed just weeks earlier when the protective cover over the spacecraft did not come off. Mariner 4 spent more than seven months travelling to Mars. On 14 and 15 July 1965, it flew past the planet, coming within about 10,000 kilometres of the surface, and took the first close-up photographs of another planet from space.

Today your phone can send a photo across the world in a second. Mariner 4 was very different. Its camera stored the pictures on a tape recorder, and the spacecraft then radioed them home at about 8 bits per second. That is so slow that each small black-and-white picture took many hours to arrive, and the whole set of about 21 pictures, plus part of a 22nd, took more than a week.

Engineers at JPL were too excited to wait for the computers to turn the first numbers into an image. So they printed out the brightness numbers on strips of paper, pinned them to a board and coloured them in by hand with pastel crayons, like a giant paint-by-numbers. That hand-coloured first picture of Mars was framed and given to JPL's director, William Pickering, and it is still a wonderful reminder of how eager people were to see.

The pictures were a shock. Instead of canals and green fields, they showed a dusty, cratered landscape that looked more like the Moon. Mariner 4 also measured the air by watching how its radio signal changed as the spacecraft passed behind the planet. The atmosphere turned out to be extremely thin, less than one percent as thick as Earth's. Mars was colder, drier and emptier than the dreamers had hoped. Mariner 4 kept working long after its flyby, travelling around the Sun for about three more years and studying the solar wind.

sections.heading: Voyager's Grand Tour and the Planet Slingshot
paragraphs: In the 1960s, a young mathematician named Michael Minovitch, working at JPL as a summer student, and other scientists studied a clever trick that would change space exploration: the gravity assist. NASA engineers then noticed something rare coming up in the late 1970s. Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune would be lined up on the same side of the Sun in a way that happens only about once every 175 years. A spacecraft launched at the right time could visit all four, using each planet to fling it on to the next.

Here is how a gravity assist works, explained simply. Imagine a tennis ball thrown at the front of a moving train. The ball bounces off the train much faster than it was thrown, because it picks up some of the train's speed. A spacecraft does something similar with a planet, except it never touches the planet. Gravity does the bouncing. The spacecraft sails close behind the planet as the planet moves along its orbit around the Sun. The planet's gravity swings the craft around and sends it off in a new direction, carrying away a little of the planet's orbital energy. The planet slows down by an amount far too tiny to ever measure, but the small spacecraft gains a huge boost.

Twin spacecraft were built for the journey: Voyager 1 and Voyager 2. Each was about the size of a small car, with a big white dish antenna 3.7 metres across. They were too far from the Sun to use solar panels, so each carried three generators powered by the heat of decaying plutonium. Voyager 2 actually launched first, on 20 August 1977. Voyager 1 followed on 5 September 1977 on a faster path, overtaking its twin and reaching Jupiter first.

The Voyagers' pictures amazed the world. Voyager 1 passed Jupiter in March 1979 and discovered active volcanoes on its moon Io, the first erupting volcanoes ever seen anywhere beyond Earth. It found thin rings around Jupiter, too. It reached Saturn in November 1980, and swung close to Saturn's giant moon Titan, which turned out to have a thick, hazy atmosphere mostly made of nitrogen. That close look at Titan bent Voyager 1's path up and out of the plane of the planets, so it could not visit any more worlds.

Voyager 2 carried on with the grand tour. After Jupiter (1979) and Saturn (1981), it became the first, and so far the only, spacecraft to visit Uranus (January 1986) and Neptune (August 1989). It found new moons and rings and showed Neptune's dark storms and its icy moon Triton, where geysers seemed to spray dark material into the thin air. Everything we have seen up close of those two distant blue worlds comes from that one spacecraft.

On 14 February 1990, Voyager 1 turned its camera back toward home and took a family portrait of the planets. In one frame, Earth is a tiny speck less than a single pixel wide, floating in a beam of scattered sunlight. Carl Sagan called it the 'Pale Blue Dot'.

In August 2012, Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause, the edge of the bubble of solar wind that surrounds our solar system, and entered interstellar space: the space between the stars. Voyager 2 followed in November 2018. They are the most distant human-made objects ever. Voyager 1 is so far away that its radio signals, travelling at the speed of light, take almost a whole day to reach us, and NASA expects it to pass one full light-day from Earth around November 2026. Their power is slowly running down, and engineers have been switching off instruments one by one to keep them talking a little longer.

sections.heading: Touching Down on Mars: Mars 3, Viking and Sojourner
paragraphs: Flying past a planet is hard. Landing on Mars is much harder. Mars has enough air to make a spacecraft glow red-hot as it plunges in, but far too little air for parachutes to slow it down fully. Engineers have to combine a heat shield, a parachute and then something else, such as rockets or airbags, to finish the job. Everything must happen automatically, because radio signals take minutes to cross the gap and there is no time for anyone on Earth to steer.

The Soviet Union tried first. In late 1971, two Soviet spacecraft, Mars 2 and Mars 3, arrived just as a huge dust storm was raging across the whole planet. The Mars 2 lander crashed on 27 November 1971, becoming the first human-made object to reach the surface of Mars, though not in one piece. On 2 December 1971, the Mars 3 lander came down safely, becoming the first spacecraft to make a soft landing on Mars. It began to transmit, but after only about 20 seconds the signal stopped and never returned. It was a real first, but a heartbreaking one.

NASA's turn came with the Viking program. Two Vikings were launched in 1975, each made of an orbiter and a lander. The orbiters circled the planet and scouted for safe landing places. On 20 July 1976, exactly seven years after Apollo 11's Eagle touched down on the Moon, the Viking 1 lander settled onto a plain called Chryse Planitia, slowed by a heat shield, a parachute and finally three small rocket engines. Within minutes it began sending the first picture ever taken from the surface of Mars: a view of one of its own footpads resting in the dusty, rocky soil.

After Viking, more than twenty years passed before anything else landed successfully on Mars. Then, on 4 July 1997, NASA's Mars Pathfinder arrived in a startling new way. Instead of a gentle rocket landing, it was wrapped in giant airbags, like a bundle of beach balls. After the parachute and rockets slowed it, Pathfinder dropped to the ground and bounced across the surface many times before rolling to a stop. Then the airbags deflated, the lander opened its petals like a flower, and out rolled the first rover ever to drive on Mars.

That rover was called Sojourner, named after Sojourner Truth, the American campaigner against slavery and for women's rights. It was tiny: about the size of a microwave oven and weighing only about 11 kilograms. Sojourner was designed to work for a week but kept going for nearly three months, inching around the landing site, studying rocks that the team gave friendly names such as Barnacle Bill and Yogi.

sections.heading: Spirit and Opportunity: Rovers That Would Not Quit
paragraphs: Sojourner proved that a rover could work on Mars. The next step was to build real robot geologists that could drive far and study rocks like a scientist would. NASA built twin rovers, each about the size of a golf cart, with six wheels, a mast topped with stereo cameras like eyes, and a robotic arm carrying a microscope, spectrometers and a tool that could grind into rocks. They were named Spirit and Opportunity by a third-grade girl, Sofi Collis, who won a naming contest. She had once lived in an orphanage in Russia before being adopted and wrote that America gave her the opportunity to make her dreams come true.

Both rovers landed using Pathfinder-style airbags. Spirit came down in Gusev Crater on 4 January 2004. Three weeks later, on the other side of the planet, Opportunity bounced and rolled straight into a small crater on the flat plain of Meridiani Planum. Scientists joked it was a 'hole in one', because the walls of that little crater showed layers of rock right in front of the rover's cameras.

Each rover was designed for a mission of 90 Martian days, called sols (a sol is about 40 minutes longer than an Earth day). Engineers expected dust to slowly cover their solar panels until they ran out of power. But something lucky happened: Martian winds and small whirlwinds called dust devils sometimes swept across the rovers and blew their panels clean. Again and again, the rovers' power came back.

Spirit explored the hills of Gusev Crater for more than five years. When one of its front wheels stopped working in 2006, the team drove it backwards, dragging the broken wheel. That accident turned out to be useful: the dragging wheel scraped up bright soil that was almost pure silica, a material that on Earth often forms around hot springs. It was a strong clue that hot water had once flowed there. In 2009 Spirit got stuck in soft sand and could not escape. It kept working as a stationary science station until it fell silent in March 2010, and NASA officially ended its mission in May 2011.

Opportunity kept rolling. Soon after landing, it found small round grains of a mineral called hematite, nicknamed 'blueberries', and layers of rock that could only have formed in water. This was some of the strongest evidence yet that liquid water had once soaked the surface of Mars. Later, the rover drove for years to reach the rim of Endeavour Crater, about 22 kilometres across, where it found signs of ancient water that was not too acidic, the kind of water that living things might have been able to use.

Then, in June 2018, a dust storm swelled until it wrapped the entire planet. The sky above Opportunity grew so dark that its solar panels could no longer make enough electricity. Its last message arrived on 10 June 2018. For eight months the team sent more than a thousand commands, hoping the wind would clean its panels once more. On 13 February 2019, NASA announced the mission was over. A rover meant to last 90 days had worked for almost 15 years.

sections.heading: Sky Cranes, Perseverance and a Helicopter on Mars
paragraphs: NASA's next rover, Curiosity, was too big for airbags. It is about the size of a small car and weighs about 900 kilograms, roughly five times as much as Spirit or Opportunity. Instead of solar panels, it runs on a nuclear generator that turns the heat of decaying plutonium into electricity, so dust storms and winter do not stop it. But how do you gently set down a one-tonne robot on a planet with hardly any air?

JPL engineers invented a daring answer: the sky crane. After the heat shield and an enormous parachute had slowed the spacecraft, a rocket-powered descent stage dropped free and hovered above the ground like a jet-pack. Then it lowered Curiosity on nylon cables several metres long, until the rover's wheels touched the ground. The cables were cut, and the descent stage flew off to crash safely some distance away. The whole sequence, from hitting the top of the atmosphere to standing on the ground, took about seven minutes, all carried out by the spacecraft's computers on their own. Engineers called it the 'seven minutes of terror'.

It worked perfectly. Curiosity landed in Gale Crater on 6 August 2012 (the evening of 5 August in California), and the control room at JPL erupted in cheers and hugs. Not long afterwards, the rover found that Gale Crater once held a lake of fresh water, with the chemical ingredients that microbes on Earth would need. Later it detected organic molecules, carbon-based chemicals that are building blocks for life (although they can also form without life), and seasonal changes in a gas called methane. Curiosity is still climbing the slopes of Mount Sharp, a mountain of layered rock in the middle of the crater, reading the history of Mars layer by layer like the pages of a book.

Its bigger cousin, Perseverance, launched on 30 July 2020 and landed on 18 February 2021 using the same sky crane, plus a new trick: a camera system that compared pictures of the ground with a map and steered toward a safe spot. Perseverance landed in Jezero Crater, which billions of years ago held a lake fed by a river. The river left behind a fan-shaped delta of mud and sand, just the kind of place where signs of ancient life might be preserved.

Tucked under Perseverance's belly was the most charming passenger of all: a small helicopter named Ingenuity. It weighed only about 1.8 kilograms on Earth and had two rotors, each about 1.2 metres across, spinning in opposite directions very fast, roughly 2,400 times a minute, because the thin Martian air gives so little to push against. Flying on Mars is like flying on Earth at nearly 30 kilometres high, far above where any normal helicopter can go.

On 19 April 2021, Ingenuity lifted off, rose about 3 metres, hovered, turned and landed again. The flight lasted about 39 seconds, but it was the first powered, controlled flight of an aircraft on another planet. The helicopter carried a postage-stamp-sized piece of fabric from the Wright brothers' 1903 Flyer, linking the first flight on Earth with the first flight on Mars, and the team named the take-off spot Wright Brothers Field.

Ingenuity was built as a quick experiment of up to five flights in about a month. Instead it flew 72 times between 2021 and 2024, travelling roughly 17 kilometres in total and spending more than two hours in the air. It became a scout, flying ahead to show the rover's drivers the best routes. On its 72nd flight, on 18 January 2024, it came down hard and damaged its rotor blades, possibly because the smooth, featureless sand confused its navigation camera. NASA ended its mission that month. Its success means future Mars missions will probably carry flying scouts of their own.

sections.heading: New Flags at Mars, and Why Mars Is So Hard
paragraphs: India's Mars Orbiter Mission, nicknamed Mangalyaan ('Mars craft' in Hindi), launched on 5 November 2013 from Sriharikota on India's PSLV rocket. On 24 September 2014, after a journey of about 300 days and roughly 670 million kilometres, it fired its engine and slipped into orbit around Mars. India became the first country to reach Mars orbit on its very first try. The mission cost about 74 million US dollars, famously less than the budget of some Hollywood space films. Mangalyaan kept working for about eight years.

In July 2020, three missions set off for Mars in the same few weeks, because that was when the planets were in the right positions. The United Arab Emirates launched its Hope orbiter on a Japanese H-IIA rocket from Tanegashima, Japan, on 20 July 2020. Hope reached Mars orbit on 9 February 2021, making it the first interplanetary mission from an Arab country. Its special orbit lets it watch Martian weather at every time of day, like a weather satellite for another planet.

China's Tianwen-1 ('Questions to Heaven') arrived in Mars orbit the next day, on 10 February 2021. Its mission carried an orbiter, a lander and a rover all at once, something no country had done on its first Mars trip. In May 2021, the lander touched down on Utopia Planitia, the same broad plain where Viking 2 had landed 45 years before, and the rover Zhurong, named after a fire god in Chinese mythology, rolled onto the surface. China became the second country, after the United States, to drive a rover on Mars. Zhurong was designed for 90 sols and worked for about a year, studying the ground with radar, before it went into hibernation for the harsh Martian winter in May 2022 and did not wake up.

Why is Mars so difficult? First, timing. Earth and Mars both circle the Sun, Earth on the inside track moving faster. The most fuel-saving path from one to the other is a long curving arc that takes about seven months, and it only lines up roughly every 26 months. Miss that launch window and you wait more than two years for the next one. That is why so many Mars missions launch together in bursts, such as the three in July 2020.

Second, distance and delay. The distance between Earth and Mars changes from about 55 million kilometres at the closest to around 400 million kilometres when they are on opposite sides of the Sun. Radio waves travel at the speed of light, but even so a message takes from about 3 minutes to more than 20 minutes to cross, one way. You cannot drive a Mars rover with a joystick like a video game. Engineers send a whole day's instructions at once and wait to see what happened, and landings must be completely automatic.

Third, the air. Mars's atmosphere is less than one percent as thick as Earth's at the surface. It is thick enough to cause dangerous heating during entry, but too thin for parachutes alone to slow a heavy spacecraft. Landing larger and larger loads, such as one day a ship carrying people, is one of the biggest unsolved engineering problems in spaceflight.

Fourth, radiation and cold. Mars has no global magnetic field and only a thin atmosphere, so far more harmful radiation from the Sun and from deep space reaches the surface than on Earth. Nights are colder than Antarctica. Machines must be built to survive it, and future astronauts would need shelter.

It is no wonder that, by 2014, only around 21 of 51 missions sent toward Mars had succeeded, as India's prime minister pointed out when Mangalyaan arrived. Every success was built on lessons learned from failures. And all of these brave robot explorers had one thing in common: the rockets that launched them were used once and then thrown away, falling into the ocean or burning up in the sky. Every mission meant building a whole new rocket from scratch, which is a little like throwing away an airliner after one flight. Then a young company decided to do something that many experts thought was impossible: land its rockets and fly them again.

deepDive: Getting to Mars is less about raw speed than about clever timing. The most fuel-efficient route between two planets is called a Hohmann transfer orbit: a half-ellipse around the Sun that just touches Earth's orbit at one end and Mars's orbit at the other. For Mars that trip takes roughly 7 to 9 months. The launch must be timed so that Mars arrives at the far end of the ellipse at the same moment as the spacecraft. Because Earth laps Mars about once every 780 days (the synodic period, about 26 months), that alignment repeats only that often. Missions can take faster, more curved paths, but every extra bit of speed costs fuel, and fuel costs mass, which, as the rocket equation shows, grows very quickly. Gravity assists are the other big money-saver of planetary travel. Relative to the planet, a spacecraft leaves a flyby with the same speed it arrived with; only its direction changes. But measured relative to the Sun, that change in direction can add or remove several kilometres per second, borrowed from the planet's orbital motion. Voyager 2 more than doubled its speed through flybys of Jupiter, Saturn and Uranus. Without such slingshots, reaching the outer planets in a reasonable time would need far bigger rockets than exist. Landing is the third great challenge. Engineers call it EDL: entry, descent and landing. Mars's thin atmosphere removes most of a probe's speed during entry, but the supersonic parachutes used since Viking become less useful as payloads grow heavier, and Curiosity and Perseverance, at around one tonne, are close to the practical limit of today's methods. Landing the tens of tonnes that a human expedition would need may require new ideas such as inflatable heat shields or rocket engines fired against the oncoming supersonic air. There is also a long-running scientific debate about life. Viking's Labeled Release experiment gave results that looked biological to its designer, Gilbert Levin, but most researchers attribute them to reactive chemicals such as perchlorates, which the Phoenix lander found in Martian soil in 2008. Perseverance's sealed samples were collected partly to settle questions like this in Earth laboratories, if a return mission is ever flown.
